newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Somerfield profits up, margins eyed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Somerfield profits up, margins eyed.

text.p: British second-tier supermarket group Somerfield Plc turned in a rise in its first annual results since flotation and said it was eyeing further improvements in margins and sales.
"The current year has started well and operating margins continue to improve," chief executive David Simons told Reuters.

Pre-tax profits for the year ending April 26 were 105.4 million pounds ($176.8 million), up from pro forma profits of 92 million a year ago and at the top end of expectations, with a total dividend payout of 10.2 pence per share.
Operating margins improved to 3.6 percent compared with 3.2 percent a year ago and Simons said "we expect operating margins to improve to between say four and five percent."
But he added that there was no timescale for achieving that target.
Somerfield said total sales in the first eight weeks of the current year were up 1.6 percent in volume while food prices fell 1.4 percent.
Sales at its Somerfield fascia stores are currently up 2.8 percent in volume terms, compared with a 2.2 percent rise last year, stripping out the impact of inflation at 1.8 percent.
Somerfield added that the rate of decline in sales at its Food Giant chain and unconverted stores had slowed, from falls of eight percent and 5.4 percent respectively last year.
Simons said he saw consumer demand for food "relatively steady. It is not euphoric by any stretch of the imagination but we are seeing steady growth."
But analysts were concerned over future sales growth for the group with few new store openings and an increasingly competitive market.
Shares slipped back to be down 5.5 pence at 190 pence after recent gains ahead of the results.
"A lot of what Somerfield is doing is very good...but they are running very hard to stand still," said Clive Black, analyst at Charterhouse Tilney.

Simons said that gross margin had improved by one percentage point during the last year, helped by an improved product mix, an emphasis on fresh foods and own label and better support from suppliers for promotional campaigns.
"The outlook for gross margins in the sector was confirmed to be reasonably positive," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

There have been concerns recently that the market leaders -- Tesco, J. Sainsbury, Safeway and ASDA -- have been able to boost sales by encroaching on the traditional territory of smaller stores such as Somerfield.
But Simons said the company aimed to "complement rather than compete" with large, out-of-town superstores with its largely local, neighbourhood locations.

"We have a very clear customer base which is actually quite different from the out-of-town superstore," he said, adding that Somerfield attracted top-up shoppers and those who do their main shop in more than one visit.
Somerfield also had primary customers who might not want to go to out-of-town stores because they are too big, inconvenient to reach or too impersonal, he added.

The company intends to open seven stores this year with total investment of 130-140 million pounds, up from 104 million last year. But Simons said he anticipated growth in sales from improvement in volumes and operating margins at its existing 600 stores.
